steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper studying how label noise in pre-training data affects pre-trained models on downstream tasks, and how to mitigate it with light-weight black-box fine-tuning. Motivate the problem, state the research questions, and summarize our findings and method.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- The pre-training and fine-tuning (PT-FT) paradigm
- What determines downstream performance: fine-tuning efforts and pre-training data
- Label noise in large-scale pre-training data as the motivating case
- Our problem and how it differs from noisy label learning
- Key questions and findings: influence, analysis, mitigation
- Broader outlook: Noisy Model Learning

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- PT-FT paradigm
  - de facto standard in deep learning
  - vs. training from scratch per task (time-consuming, resource-intensive, less adaptable)
  - pre-train larger general model on huge datasets, transfer (foundation model) to downstream tasks
  - ResNet, Vision Transformers pre-trained on ImageNet and larger, potentially noisy datasets
  - also NLP and multi-modality; pre-training on web-scraped data
- Downstream performance
  - generalization/transferability not guaranteed; cause in pre-training or fine-tuning
  - fine-tuning work: OOD generalization, semi-supervised, imbalanced, noisy label learning
  - scaling pre-training data helps, but distribution matters too
  - recent work: quality more important than quantity for robust generalization
  - bias from collection/annotation (corrupted, poisoned, false info) -> malicious influence downstream
- Label noise example
  - CLIP on LAION-2B (billion-scale, uncurated) only matches CLIP on WIT-400M (cleaned by OpenAI)
  - noise from human annotators and web crawlers; hard to avoid in pre-training
  - models pre-trained on noisy data: Noisy Student, BiT, Open CLIP; noisy raw text for BERT, GPT
  - growing models/datasets -> important and challenging to understand noise effects
- Our problem
  - first study: understand label noise in pre-training data, effects downstream, mitigate
  - differs from noisy label learning: noise in (black-box) pre-training data; no noise assumptions on downstream data (combinable, Section 4.3; Section 5)
  - hard to alter pre-training or fully fine-tune -> careful fine-tuning given a pre-trained model
- Questions (supervised pre-training)
  - Influence: ResNet-50, fully-supervised and contrastive, noisy ImageNet-1K and YFCC15M, ratios 0,5\%,10\%,20\%,30\%; ID: slight noise (up to 5\% or 10\%) helps; OOD: even 5\% hurts (Figures 1, 2)
  - Analysis: singular value spectrum (Section 2.3); smaller largest singular value, flatter distribution, higher dimension span; helps ID at first, then fits noise; dominant singular values down -> less OOD transferability (Figure 3)
  - Mitigation: black-box fine-tuning, three regularization objectives on singular value spectrum (Section 3); noisy ResNet-50 (Figure 1); noisy pre-trained models and APIs, vision and language (Section 4)
- Outlook
  - Noisy Model Learning (NML), complementary to noisy label learning
  - era of foundation models: users only have weights or APIs
  - adapting without full fine-tuning; e.g. detection/segmentation in medical and autonomous driving

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The transfer learning paradigm of pre-training and fine-tuning (PT-FT) is now the de facto standard in deep learning research and application today. Training a neural network from scratch for each individual task can be time-consuming, resource-intensive, and less adaptable, so instead the PT-FT paradigm first pre-trains a relatively larger and more general model on huge volumes of data, and then transfers this pre-trained model (or the foundation model) to different downstream tasks. For example, ResNet and Vision Transformers pre-trained on ImageNet and on larger but possibly noisy datasets are widely used in computer vision. The PT-FT paradigm is also predominant in natural language processing and multi-modality, where pre-training is usually done on large datasets scraped from the web.

The generalization and transferability of pre-trained models on downstream tasks are usually not guaranteed to be satisfying, and the reason can be in the pre-training or in the fine-tuning. Over the years there has been a lot of effort to improve fine-tuning performance in different practical downstream scenarios, for example out-of-distribution generalization, semi-supervised learning, imbalanced learning, and noisy label learning. It is commonly believed that scaling up the size of the pre-training data helps downstream performance, but the distribution of the data also plays an essential role. Recently, one study and another study found that the quality of pre-training data matters more than the quantity for robust generalization. Bias in the pre-training data that comes from the collection (and annotation) process, e.g., corrupted, poisoned, and false information, can also have malicious and unexpected influence on downstream tasks.

Label noise is one example. Training CLIP on LAION-2B, a billion-scale uncurated image-text pair dataset, only matches the performance of training it on WIT-400M, which is heavily cleaned and processed by OpenAI. Label noise in large-scale datasets inevitably exists because of the data collection process by human annotators and web crawlers. So it can be hard to avoid or eliminate in pre-training. Actually, many models have already been pre-trained on large-scale noisy data and transferred to downstream tasks, such as Noisy Student, BiT, and Open CLIP. There is also the enormous but noisy raw text used to pre-train language models such as BERT and GPT. As pre-trained models and datasets have grown significantly, it has become more and more important, and more challenging, to understand how noise in pre-training data affects the performance of pre-trained models on downstream tasks.

This paper is the first study on this unexplored problem: we try to understand the label noise in pre-training data, understand its effects on downstream tasks, and then mitigate these (malignant) effects. There are existing efforts called "noisy label learning" that train a robust model given noisy training data. Our problem is different because the noisy labels are in the (usually black-box) pre-training data, and we do not make noise assumptions on the downstream data (although they can be used together, as in Section 4.3; more discussion is in Section 5). Because pre-trained models and datasets keep getting bigger, it is very difficult to change the pre-training process or fine-tune the entire models (they are black-box, or cannot be updated because of the large parameter size and limited computation). So, given a pre-trained model, we should take special care in fine-tuning to overcome the influence of noise in pre-training on downstream tasks.

Our study tries to answer these key questions: 1) Influence: Does noise in pre-training data influence downstream performance? 2) Analysis: Why does this influence happen? and 3) Mitigation: How can we mitigate this influence in a light-weight, black-box fine-tuning process? We give an in-depth analysis to answer these questions, based on the popular supervised pre-training paradigm.

- Our questions (supervised pre-training paradigm)
  - Influence: benevolent and malignant
    - ResNet-50, fully-supervised and contrastive, synthetic noisy ImageNet-1K and YFCC15M, ratios 0,5\%,10\%,20\%,30\% (Sections 2.1, 2.2)
    - ID: slight noise (up to 5\% or 10\%) benefits; OOD: even 5\% drastically hurts (Figure 1, Figure 2)
  - Analysis: noise shapes feature space
    - singular value spectrum (Section 2.3): smaller largest singular value, flatter distribution, higher dimension span
    - initial increase helps ID, further increase fits noise structure
    - smaller dominant singular values -> less OOD transferability (Figure 3)
  - Mitigation: simple black-box fine-tuning to reshape feature space
    - three regularization objectives on singular value spectrum (Section 3)
    - noisy ResNet-50 (Figure 1); popular noisy pre-trained models and APIs, vision and language (Section 4)
- Outlook
  - new topic, complementary to noisy label learning: Noisy Model Learning (NML)
  - more significant with large foundation models; users only have weights or APIs
  - removing malignant influence without full fine-tuning; detection/segmentation in medical and autonomous driving
  - hope: better understanding and application of foundation models

steps.text:

For example, ResNet and Vision Transformers pre-trained on ImageNet and on larger but possibly noisy datasets are widely used in computer vision. The PT-FT paradigm is also predominant in natural language processing and multi-modality, where pre-training is usually done on large datasets scraped from the web.

Bias in the pre-training data that comes from the collection (and annotation) process, e.g., corrupted, poisoned, and false information, can also have malicious and unexpected influence on downstream tasks.

Training CLIP on LAION-2B, a billion-scale uncurated image-text pair dataset, only matches the performance of training it on WIT-400M, which is heavily cleaned and processed by OpenAI. Label noise in large-scale datasets inevitably exists because of the data collection process by human annotators and web crawlers. So it can be hard to avoid or eliminate in pre-training. Actually, many models have already been pre-trained on large-scale noisy data and transferred to downstream tasks, such as Noisy Student, BiT, and Open CLIP. There is also the enormous but noisy raw text used to pre-train language models such as BERT and GPT. As pre-trained models and datasets have grown significantly, it has become more and more important, and more challenging, to understand how noise in pre-training data affects the performance of pre-trained models on downstream tasks.

This paper is the first study on this unexplored problem: we try to understand the label noise in pre-training data, understand its effects on downstream tasks, and then mitigate these (malignant) effects. There are existing efforts called "noisy label learning" that train a robust model given noisy training data. Our problem is different because the noisy labels are in the (usually black-box) pre-training data, and we do not make noise assumptions on the downstream data (although they can be used together, as in Section 4.3; more discussion is in Section 5). Because pre-trained models and datasets keep getting bigger, it is very difficult to change the pre-training process or fine-tune the entire models (they are black-box, or cannot be updated because of the large parameter size and limited computation). So, given a pre-trained model, we should take special care in fine-tuning to overcome the influence of noise in pre-training on downstream tasks.

Our study tries to answer these key questions: 1) Influence: Does noise in pre-training data influence downstream performance? 2) Analysis: Why does this influence happen? and 3) Mitigation: How can we mitigate this influence in a light-weight, black-box fine-tuning process? We give an in-depth analysis to answer these questions, based on the popular supervised pre-training paradigm.

- Influence: Label noise in pre-training data has both benevolent and malignant influence on downstream tasks. In Sections 2.1 and 2.2, we run realistic experiments with ResNet-50 models that are fully-supervised and contrastive pre-trained on synthetic noisy ImageNet-1K and YFCC15M with different noise ratios (0,5\%,10\%,20\%,30\%), and then we study generalization performance on downstream in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) tasks. We see that on ID tasks a little noise (up to 5\% or 10\%) can help generalization performance. But even 5\% noise can drastically hurt robustness and transferability on OOD tasks, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

- Analysis: Label noise in pre-training shapes the feature space of the pre-trained model a lot. In Section 2.3, we do an empirical analysis of the singular value spectrum of the feature space of the pre-trained models. Noise in pre-training leads to a smaller largest singular value and a flatter singular value distribution with a higher dimension span in the feature space. At first an increase in the spanning dimension of the feature space helps discriminability on ID tasks. But it then becomes harmful as it increases more, which means more feature capacity is learned to fit the noise structure. The decrease in the dominant singular values leads to less transferability for OOD tasks, as shown in Figure 3.

- Mitigation: We design a simple black-box fine-tuning algorithm that reshapes the pre-trained feature space, so it reduces the influence of noisy pre-training data and boosts downstream performance. In Section 3, based on the analysis, we propose three regularization objectives on the singular value spectrum that help affine the feature space. We show that the proposed method is effective on noisy ResNet-50 models with extensive analysis, as shown in Figure 1. In Section 4, we validate our method further on popular noisy pre-trained models (and APIs) and show superior generalization performance on both vision and language tasks.

Beyond our analysis, we see this research as a new topic complementary to the classic noisy label learning setting, which we call Noisy Model Learning (NML). We think this direction is even more valuable in the era of large foundation models, where downstream users only have access to model weights or APIs. It would be especially interesting to explore how to remove the malignant influence of noise in pre-training on downstream tasks when adapting these models without full fine-tuning, since this may exist in broader applications such as detection and segmentation in medical and autonomous driving. We hope future research on this topic can help a better understanding and application of large foundation models.

steps.text:
The transfer learning paradigm of pre-training and fine-tuning (PT-FT) [1] has become the de facto standard in today's deep learning research and application. Instead of training a neural network from scratch for each individual task, which can be time-consuming, resource-intensive, and less adaptable, the PT-FT paradigm first pre-trains a relatively larger and more general model on huge volumes of data, and then transfers this pre-trained model (or the foundation model [2]) to various downstream tasks [3,4,5,6]. For instance, ResNet [7] and Vision Transformers [8] pre-trained on ImageNet [9] and on larger but potentially noisy datasets [10,11,12] have been widely adopted in computer vision. The PT-FT paradigm has also become predominant in natural language processing [13,14,15,16,6,17,18] and multi-modality [4,19], where pre-training is usually done on large datasets scraped from the web.

The generalization and transferability of pre-trained models are usually not guaranteed to be satisfying on downstream tasks, and the reason can lie in either the pre-training or the fine-tuning. Over the years, there have been tremendous efforts to improve fine-tuning performance in various practical downstream scenarios: out-of-distribution generalization [20,21], semi-supervised learning [22,23], imbalanced learning [24,25], and noisy label learning [26,27], to name a few. While it is commonly believed that scaling up the size of the pre-training data benefits downstream performance [28], its distribution also plays an essential role [29,30]. Recently, [31] and [32] found that the quality of the pre-training data matters more than its quantity for robust generalization. Bias in pre-training data created by the collection (and annotation) process, e.g., corrupted, poisoned, and false information [33,34], can also exert malicious and unexpected influence on downstream tasks [2].

Take label noise as an example. Training CLIP [4] on LAION-2B [19], a billion-scale uncurated image-text pair dataset, can only match the performance of training it on WIT-400M [4], which is heavily cleaned and processed by OpenAI. Label noise inevitably exists in large-scale datasets owing to the data collection process by human annotators and web crawlers, and it can thus be difficult to avoid or eliminate in pre-training [12,35,19]. In fact, numerous models have already been pre-trained on large-scale noisy data and transferred to downstream tasks, such as Noisy Student [11], BiT [10], and Open CLIP [36], not to mention the enormous but noisy raw text [37,32] used to pre-train language models such as BERT [13] and GPT [16,6]. As pre-trained models and datasets grow significantly, it has become increasingly important and challenging to understand how noise in pre-training data affects the performance of pre-trained models on downstream tasks.

This paper presents the first study on this unexplored problem, demystifying the label noise in pre-training data, understanding its effects on downstream tasks, and then mitigating such (malignant) effects. Notably, existing efforts under the name of "noisy label learning" train a robust model given noisy training data [38,39,40]. Our problem is inherently different, since the noisy labels exist in the (usually black-box) pre-training data, and we make no noise assumptions on the downstream data (although the two can be used together, as in Section 4.3; more discussion is in Section 5). Due to the increasing size of pre-trained models and datasets, it is notoriously difficult to alter the pre-training process or fine-tune the entire models (they are black-box or cannot be updated due to the large parameter size and constrained computation). Therefore, given a pre-trained model, special care should be taken in fine-tuning to overcome the influence of noise in pre-training on downstream tasks.

Our study aims to answer the following key questions: 1) Influence: Does noise in pre-training data influence downstream performance? 2) Analysis: Why does such influence happen? and 3) Mitigation: How can such influence be mitigated in a light-weight, black-box fine-tuning process? We present an in-depth analysis to answer these questions, based on the popular supervised pre-training paradigm.

- Influence: The label noise in pre-training data has both benevolent and malignant influence on downstream tasks. In Sections 2.1 and 2.2, we conduct realistic experiments with ResNet-50 models [7] fully-supervised and contrastive pre-trained on synthetic noisy ImageNet-1K and YFCC15M [42] with various noise ratios (0,5\%,10\%,20\%,30\%), and then study generalization performance on downstream in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) tasks. We observe that on ID tasks, slight noise (up to 5\% or 10\%) can benefit generalization performance. In contrast, even 5\% noise can drastically deteriorate robustness and transferability on OOD tasks, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

- Analysis: The label noise in pre-training significantly shapes the feature space of the pre-trained model. In Section 2.3, we conduct an empirical analysis of the singular value spectrum of the feature space of the pre-trained models. Noise in pre-training results in a decreasing largest singular value and a flatter singular value distribution with a higher dimension span in the feature space. An initial increase in the spanning dimension of the feature space benefits discriminability on ID tasks, but further increase becomes detrimental, indicating that more feature capacity is learned to fit the noise structure. The decrease in the dominant singular values leads to less transferability for OOD tasks [43], as shown in Figure 3.

- Mitigation: We design a simple black-box fine-tuning algorithm that reshapes the pre-trained feature space, reducing the influence of noisy pre-training data and boosting the performance of downstream tasks. In Section 3, based on the analysis, we propose three regularization objectives on the singular value spectrum that help affine the feature space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on noisy ResNet-50 models with extensive analysis, as shown in Figure 1. In Section 4, we further validate our method on popular noisy pre-trained models (and APIs) and present superior generalization performance on both vision and language tasks.

Beyond our analysis, we view this research as a novel topic complementary to the classic noisy label learning setting, which we term Noisy Model Learning (NML). We believe this direction is even more significant in the era of large foundation models [2], where downstream users only have access to the model weights or APIs. It would be of particular interest to explore how to eliminate the malignant influence of noise in pre-training on downstream tasks when adapting these models without full fine-tuning, since it may exist in broader applications such as detection and segmentation in medical and autonomous driving. We hope that future research on this topic can facilitate a better understanding and application of large foundation models.
